newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Ford Motor Co sees breaking even in Vietnam by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Ford Motor Co sees breaking even in Vietnam by 2000.

text.p: U.S. automotive giant Ford Motor Company said on Friday it expects to break even in Vietnam by the year 2000 despite what analysts say is an overcrowded market.

In an interview in Hanoi, Ford's executive vice president, Wayne Booker, dismissed industry concerns over problems facing manufacturers in Vietnam and said the company's first locally made vehicle would roll off the production line within a year.
"Some manufacturers say they were told there'd be just four of them allowed here, but not us," he said. "So all along we've known it's going to be wide open. It's not shocking to us."
Hanoi has licensed some 14 foreign manufacturers, including Ford, to produce vehicles in Vietnam for the local market. Current demand for new cars is barely 10,000 units a year.
But Booker said Ford's $102 million plant, now being built near Hanoi, would produce commercial vehicles including its Transit Van rather than passenger cars until the market was better developed.
"It will break even before 2000," he said. "Any manufacturer who can't make profits by 2000 oughtn't be here."

Booker added that Ford studies announced earlier this week in Paris into the development of a new light, inexpensive mini-car for developing markets could be appropriate for Vietnam, but only after 2000.
"What it's designed to do is to move the guy off the bike to family transportation," he said. "It's somewhere between a motorcycle and a full, all-bells-ringing family car."
Vietnam's nascent auto market is currently dominated by Japanese and South Korean marques including Nissan, Mitsubishi, Daewoo and Kia.

Booker conceded that Ford's market image was hampered by memories of "V8 gas guzzlers" from the period during the Vietnam War. But he said the company had been encouraged by its progress in India and was likely to apply similar marketing to Vietnam.
He added that Ford had held limited discussions with Vietnamese officials on the possibility of exporting locally produced cars to other ASEAN countries, but did not elaborate.
"This is going to be a part of the Asia economic community and it'd be pretty difficult to leave that to the Japanese and the Koreans," he said.
